
shinyasync moves slow work off the Shiny session thread. You write the app
as you would with `reactive()`, `observe()` and `reactiveVal()`, and add
`Async` to the ones that do slow work:

| Shiny            | shinyasync            |
|------------------|-----------------------|
| `reactive()`     | `reactiveAsync()`     |
| `observe()`      | `observeAsync()`      |
| `reactiveVal()`  | `reactiveValAsync()`  |

Each one evaluates its expression on a `mirai` daemon, tracks reactive
dependencies as usual, cancels a run that a newer input has made obsolete, and
returns the previous value while the new one is computed. This article walks
through the patterns a real app needs, one at a time.

## A first app

```{r}
library(shiny)
library(shinyasync)

ui <- fluidPage(
  selectInput("x", "Predictor of mpg", c("wt", "hp", "disp", "qsec")),
  sliderInput("B", "Bootstrap resamples", 500, 5000, 2000, step = 500),
  plotOutput("slopes"),
  textOutput("status")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  slopes <- reactiveAsync({
    f <- reformulate(input$x, "mpg")    # runs in a worker, not the session
    replicate(input$B, {
      resample <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), replace = TRUE), ]
      coef(lm(f, resample))[[2]]
    })
  })

  output$slopes <- renderPlot(hist(slopes(), main = "Bootstrap slopes", xlab = "Slope"))
  output$status <- renderText(status_async(slopes))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Change the predictor while a fit is running: the run on the old predictor is
cancelled, the previous histogram stays on screen until the new one arrives,
and other users of the app are never blocked. The first task starts a daemon
pool shared by every session in the process. To size it, call `pool_async()`
at the top level of `app.R`; `vignette("deployment")` explains how to choose
the size.

The app is in the package:
`shiny::runApp(system.file("examples/quickstart", package = "shinyasync"))`.

## Spinner or previous result

While a task runs the status is `"running"` whether or not there is a previous
value on screen. `has_value_async()` tells the two apart:

```{r}
output$note <- renderUI({
  running <- status_async(slopes) == "running"
  if (running && !has_value_async(slopes)) icon("spinner", class = "fa-spin")
  else if (running) span(class = "text-muted", "Showing the previous result while the new one computes")
})
```

Before the first task is sent to a worker the status is `"initial"`, as for
an `ExtendedTask`.

## Button-triggered

Use `bindEvent()` exactly as you would with `reactive()`:

```{r}
fit <- reactiveAsync(fit_model(input$formula, data())) |>
  bindEvent(input$go)
```

A cancel button calls `cancel_async(fit)`. Afterwards the status is `"idle"`,
a status an `ExtendedTask` does not have, while `has_value_async(fit)` stays
`TRUE`, and the previous result remains on screen until the next click starts
a new task.

With bslib, `bind_task_button()` keeps an `input_task_button()` busy while the
task runs, as it does for an `ExtendedTask`:

```{r}
fit <- reactiveAsync(fit_model(input$formula, data())) |>
  bindEvent(input$go) |>
  bslib::bind_task_button("go")
```

## Hidden outputs

A task starts the first time its reactive or status is read. Shiny suspends
outputs in hidden tabs, so a task that only hidden outputs read does not start
until the tab is opened. To start it on load, as in plain Shiny:

```{r}
outputOptions(output, "forecast", suspendWhenHidden = FALSE)
```

## Debounced input

Debounce the input in a plain `reactive()` and read that:

```{r}
query <- debounce(reactive(input$query), 400)

results <- reactiveAsync(search_db(query()))
```

## Side effects

`observeAsync()` runs a side effect on a worker. Nothing reads an observer's
result, so an error is reported with `message()` and the status becomes
`"error"` until a dependency changes.

```{r}
observeAsync({
  write_audit_log(input$user, results())
})
```

There is no queue mode for observers: a dependency change cancels a running
side effect. For a write that must not be skipped, use
`reactiveAsync(..., mode = "queue")` and read its result in an output, as
`vignette("extendedtask")` shows.

## Background refresh

`invalidateLater()` runs on the session, so it re-runs the task on a timer
without blocking anything:

```{r}
dashboard <- reactiveAsync({
  invalidateLater(60e3)
  fetch_dashboard_data()
})
```

## Manual control and fan-out

`reactiveValAsync()` is the imperative counterpart: a value you set from an
observer rather than derive, as with `reactiveVal()`. `mirai_async()` starts a
task with the same capture as `reactiveAsync()` and returns the plain `mirai`
its setter accepts, so one observer can start a task per item:

```{r}
forecasts <- lapply(spots, function(spot) reactiveValAsync())

observe({
  for (i in seq_along(spots)) {
    # fetch_marine() and its helpers are shipped; input$days is a dependency.
    forecasts[[i]](mirai_async(fetch_marine(spots[[i]], days = input$days)))
  }
}) |> bindEvent(input$refresh)

output$table <- renderTable(do.call(rbind, lapply(forecasts, function(f) f())))
```

For a single button-triggered task, `reactiveAsync() |> bindEvent()` is all
you need.

## Chained async reactives

An async reactive can read another one, exactly as a `reactive()` would:

```{r}
wind   <- reactiveAsync(fetch_wind(input$spot))
scored <- reactiveAsync(score(wind(), input$spot))
```

While `wind` is catching up with a new `input$spot`, `scored` keeps its
previous value rather than combining the new spot with wind fetched for the
old one, and re-runs once `wind` has settled. That is what a chain of
`reactive()` expressions does, so nothing in the expression changes. In
detail:

- **The downstream waits.** While an upstream it reads is catching up with
  its own inputs, the downstream keeps its previous value, reports
  `"running"` while that upstream runs, and re-runs once it has settled. In
  `mode = "latest"` a run already computing on the old upstream value is
  dropped.
- **Staleness and errors follow the chain.** An error in `wind` propagates to
  `scored` on its next read.
- **An upstream gated by `bindEvent()`.** A downstream that also reads one of
  the upstream's inputs waits for the upstream's next event instead of
  recomputing with the old upstream value. Wrap the upstream read in
  `isolate()` if you want neither the wait nor the dependency.
- **A downstream gated by `bindEvent()`.** If its event fires while its
  upstream is running, it runs once the upstream settles, as a synchronous
  `reactive()` would have been ready at the click. If the upstream is stale
  but not running, the event is dropped.

## Modules

Nothing changes inside `moduleServer()`: the namespaced `input` and the
module's arguments and local functions are captured like any others, and the
async reactive can be returned to the caller.

```{r}
bootServer <- function(id, dataset, response) {
  moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    slope <- function(d, x) coef(lm(reformulate(x, response), d))[[2]]   # shipped to the worker

    slopes <- reactiveAsync(
      replicate(input$B, slope(dataset[sample(nrow(dataset), replace = TRUE), ], input$x))
    )

    output$slopes <- renderPlot(hist(slopes(), main = session$ns(""), xlab = "Slope"))
    output$status <- renderText(status_async(slopes))
    slopes
  })
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  cars <- bootServer("cars", mtcars, "mpg")
  air  <- bootServer("air", airquality, "Ozone")

  output$both <- renderText(
    sprintf("Median slopes: %.3f and %.3f", median(cars()), median(air()))
  )
}
```

The full app, with its UI, is in the package:
`shiny::runApp(system.file("examples/modules", package = "shinyasync"))`.

## A complete app

[shinyasync-example](https://github.com/dawiegriesel/shinyasync-example) is a
surf forecast dashboard that uses every primitive in the package: parallel API
fetches with stale-while-revalidate, a chained async score, a button-triggered
simulation with cancel, a background refresh, an `observeAsync()` cache writer,
a raw mirai feeding `reactiveValAsync()`, a module mounted twice, and a pool
preloaded with a request template through `pool_async(everywhere = )`. A task
monitor in the sidebar shows the status of each one.
